It all really started after the school shooting last year. I was the one who had to lock my kids in the classroom, listen to the shots in the hallway. Since then, I just haven’t been the same, and it’s been constant, not really coming and going in clear phases.

I’m on edge all the time. I can’t sit still in the staff room; I’m pacing, checking the doors, my body feels revved up like I’ve had ten coffees even when I’m exhausted. Nights are the worst. I lie there replaying the sounds, jumping at every noise. It takes me hours to fall asleep, and when I finally do, it’s light, restless. That’s been going on pretty much every night for months.

I used to love teaching, joking with the students, coaching debate. Now it all feels flat, like I’m watching myself from a distance. My head feels foggy in class; I lose my train of thought mid‑sentence. Sometimes, walking over the overpass to school, I get these sudden urges to just step off into traffic. It’s not that I’ve planned anything out, but the impulse scares me. It’s getting harder to keep functioning at work.
D008-D018_h024.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder

D008-D018_h025.question:
It really started after that car accident about a year ago—the one where the other driver died. I walked away with just bruises, but since then I haven’t felt like the same person.

I’m on edge all the time. It’s like my body is stuck in “on” mode—heart racing, muscles tight. I jump at every horn or sudden sound. At night I can’t settle; even when I’m exhausted I lie there replaying the crash, or I wake up from these vivid dreams where it’s happening again. My sleep has been messed up pretty much every night since the accident, not just here and there.

Sometimes that restlessness turns into this wired, almost giddy energy. I’ll get this rush, like I have to move, to do something, so I’ll drag my husband out late or start scrolling and buying stuff online—expensive gadgets, clothes we can’t afford. I know it’s reckless, but in the moment it feels like the only way to outrun how tense I feel. It’s not like it comes in clear “up” and “down” phases; it’s more this constant current under everything since the crash.

At work cleaning teeth, I lose track of what patients are saying, and on my days off I just want to stay in bed and not wake up at all.
D008-D018_h025.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Delusional Disorder
    D. Bipolar I Disorder
